m: The call to prayer, said out loud five times a day to tell people that a prayer time has started. It begins with “Allahu Akbar”: God is greater.
Short remembrances and prayers that Muslims say at set times, such as morning, evening and before sleep. It is the plural of dhikr.
The Hereafter: the life that comes after this one. Muslims believe every person will be brought back to life and every good deed will count.
“All praise and thanks belong to God.” People say it when something good happens, and also as a way of staying grateful when things are hard.
An Arabic word for a learned person. In Shukr, Alim is the name of the AI companion you can ask questions. It is a helpful guide, not a scholar or a fatwa source.
The Arabic word for God: the One who created everything. Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews also use the word Allah for God.
“God is greater.” It reminds the speaker that God is greater than any worry, fear or plan. It opens the call to prayer and every prayer.
“Peace be upon you.” This is the everyday Muslim greeting. The reply is “Wa alaykum assalam”, meaning “and upon you be peace”.
A verse of the Quran. The word also means “sign”, because each verse is seen as a sign that points to God. The plural is ayat.
Blessing: a quiet goodness that makes a little go a long way, whether that is time, money, food or energy.
“In the name of God.” Muslims say it before eating, travelling, starting work and before almost anything else they begin.
Remembering God, often by gently repeating short phrases such as SubhanAllah or Alhamdulillah. Many people find it calming, like a breath for the heart.
A personal prayer: talking to God in your own words, in any language, at any time, about anything at all.
A festival or celebration day. There are two Eids each year: Eid al-Fitr at the end of Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha during the season of Hajj.
The dawn prayer, the first of the five daily prayers. It is prayed between first light and sunrise.
A recorded report of what the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, did or approved of. Scholars checked the chain of people who passed each report on, and graded it by how reliable it is.
Someone who has memorised the whole Quran by heart. Millions of people around the world, including many children, have done this.
The pilgrimage to Makkah, made in a set season each year. Every adult Muslim who is physically and financially able should go at least once in their life.
Permitted or allowed. People use it most often about food and money, but it covers anything that is wholesome and lawful.
Forbidden. Examples include alcohol, pork, stealing, lying and harming others. The list of forbidden things is small compared with all that is allowed.
Memorising the Quran. People often do it slowly, a few verses a day, repeating them often.
Literally “a covering”. Today the word usually means the headscarf many Muslim women choose to wear as part of modest dress.
The Islamic calendar. It is based on the moon, so its months move through the seasons. It counts years from the Hijrah, the Prophet’s ﷺ move from Makkah to Madinah in 622 CE.
The meal that breaks the fast at sunset. It is traditionally started with dates and water, and is often shared with family, friends and neighbours.
The person who leads the prayer. It can also mean a respected religious leader of a mosque or community.
Faith: believing in the heart, affirming with the tongue and showing it through actions.
“If God wills.” Said when talking about the future, as a humble reminder that people plan but are not fully in control.
The second, quicker call said just before the prayer begins, telling people in the mosque to stand in line.
The name of the faith. It comes from a root meaning peace and submission: finding peace by turning your life towards God.
Asking God for forgiveness, often by saying “Astaghfirullah” (I ask God’s forgiveness). It is a fresh start that is always open.
“May God reward you with good.” A warm way of saying thank you.
Paradise. The Quran describes it as gardens of peace, beyond anything anyone has seen or imagined.
Also written Jumu‘ah. Friday, and the special congregational prayer held at midday on Fridays, with a short talk (khutbah) before it.

The simple cube-shaped building in Makkah that Muslims believe Abraham and his son Ishmael built for the worship of One God. Muslims everywhere face towards it in prayer. They do not worship the building itself.
A sermon or talk, given before the Friday prayer and at Eid.
Also written Mecca. The city in Arabia where the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was born and where the Kaaba stands. It is the holiest place in Islam.
“This is what God has willed.” Said when you admire something beautiful or good, to credit God for it rather than feel envy.
A mosque, which literally means a place of prostration. It is a place for prayer, learning and community, and visitors are usually very welcome.
A person who follows Islam. The word means someone who surrenders to God and finds peace in doing so.
A person chosen by God to carry His message. Muslims believe in many prophets, including Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus and, finally, Muhammad ﷺ.
The direction of the Kaaba in Makkah, which Muslims face when they pray, wherever they are in the world.
The holy book of Islam. Muslims believe it is God’s own words, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ over 23 years. It is recited in its original Arabic.
The ninth month of the Islamic calendar. Muslims fast from dawn to sunset each day, and spend more time on prayer, charity and the Quran.
Voluntary charity, given at any time and in any amount. Even a smile counts as charity, according to a hadith reported by at-Tirmidhi.
The ritual prayer, offered five times a day. It includes standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, while reciting from the Quran.
The life story of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, from his birth in Makkah to his passing in Madinah.
The declaration of faith: “There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God.” It is the first of the five pillars.
Gratitude, and the name of this app. It means noticing what you have been given, thanking the One who gave it, and using it well.
“Glorified and exalted is He.” Often said or written (SWT) after the word Allah as a mark of reverence.
“Glory be to God.” Said in moments of wonder, such as at a sunset, and as a simple dhikr.
The meal eaten before dawn on a day of fasting.
The way of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: his habits, character and teachings, which Muslims try to follow in daily life.
A chapter of the Quran. There are 114 surahs, from a few short lines to many pages long.
Explanation or commentary on the Quran. It covers what each verse means, its context and how scholars have understood it.
The rules for reciting the Quran beautifully and correctly, including how each letter sounds and where to pause.
Being mindful of God: a gentle awareness that keeps you honest and kind, even when nobody is watching.
The worldwide Muslim community: nearly two billion people from every culture, language and colour.
The “lesser pilgrimage” to Makkah. Unlike Hajj, it can be made at any time of year and is recommended rather than required.
The short washing before prayer: hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, a wipe over the head, ears and feet. It refreshes body and mind.
Obligatory yearly charity: 2.5% of savings above a set minimum (the nisab), given to people in need. It is one of the five pillars.
A symbol written after the Prophet Muhammad’s name. It means “May God bless him and grant him peace”. In English it is sometimes shortened to (pbuh): peace be upon him.
